unit: Tabitha Pratt went to work at the little house of dreams as a servant for Dr. Hugh Carrow and his wife Nell. However, after Thirza refrained from interfering with kitchen duties or Tabitha's care of Nell, Tabitha declared to her friends in the Glen that Thirza was a fine woman who understood her place. During the intense night when Nell went into labor, Tabitha waited in the kitchen with cotton wool stuffed in her ears and her apron over her head. When Thirza expressed fear that the birth might end tragically, Tabitha fiercely rejected the notion that God would rob them of Nell. unit: After moving to Grey Shutters, Nell made a lifelong pact of friendship with Isolde Pembroke in the Pembroke garden. During her school days, she was disciplined by Miss Thorne for secretly reading Ben Hur during Canadian history class, prompting her to promise to avoid foolish novels. When Miss Thorne offered her a place in a preparation class for Regent's entrance exam, Nell eagerly pursued her dream to become a schoolteacher. At Regent's Academy, she was a top contender for the academic medal alongside Hugh Carrow and Penrose Wilson, forming close friendships with Mabel Colby and Honora Hollis. Upon becoming a teacher, Nell firmly resolved never to use physical punishment, striving instead to guide her pupils with kindness and cultivate their inherent goodness as taught by Professor Rennie. Later, she achieved her first literary success when The Youth's Friend accepted a sketch she submitted, earning a ten-dollar check.

unit: In her childhood, Lorna was an intelligent, cheerful, warm, ambitious, and deeply affectionate girl loved by everyone. Tragedies and an unwanted marriage altered her public demeanor to an aloof, proud, and reserved state, erecting a protective wall between herself and others while remaining unyieldingly loyal to her family. Rose, on the other hand, shrieked and wailed enough for both of them, leaving Lorna fully occupied as she attempted to soothe and console her mother. Rose filled me with disgust, a feeling shared by all the others, yet Lorna never lost her composure. Her mother was someone she loved. Lorna was determined to qualify as a teacher if possible, and subsequently earn the funds needed to put herself through Wexcombe College. Her father had cherished that very plan—he desired that she obtain what he had forfeited. Lorna overflowed with ambition, and her mind was packed with intelligence. She attended Regent’s, where she completed two years of studies in a single year to earn her First; upon returning home, she secured the position at the Glen school.
